keyVerseText: The children which thou shalt have, after thou hast lost the other, shall say again in thine ears, The place is too strait for me: give place to me that I may dwell.
rootMeaning: The root word שָׁכֹל (shâkôl) conveys the state of being bereaved or made childless, often through loss or deprivation. Its primary sense involves miscarriage or barrenness, emphasizing a profound loss or absence, especially of offspring. The plural form שִׁכֻּלִים (shikkulîym) extends this idea to multiple instances or ongoing experience of such loss, highlighting a continual state of childlessness or bereavement beyond mere physical absence, which enriches the English gloss by underscoring the depth and persistence of loss.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Isaiah 49:20, where it is translated as "which thou shalt have after thou hast lost." This usage reflects the concept of receiving children after a period of loss or bereavement, implying restoration following desolation. The singular occurrence and its translation emphasize the contrast between previous loss and hopeful recovery, revealing the word’s thematic focus on loss followed by renewal or replacement.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שִׁכֻּלִים deepens our grasp of God’s redemptive work in the midst of human loss and barrenness. The term’s association with bereavement and childlessness points to the brokenness caused by sin and suffering in the world. Yet, its use in Isaiah 49:20 highlights God’s promise of restoration and blessing after loss, a theme central to the gospel message. This reminds believers that God is sovereign over loss and can bring new life and hope where there was despair, reflecting Christ’s work of reconciliation and renewal.
keyVerseReflection: Isaiah 49:20 states, "The children which thou shalt have, after thou hast lost the other, shall say again in thine ears, The place is too strait for me: give place to me that I may dwell." The word שִׁכֻּלִים here captures the poignant reality of losing children but also the promise of new ones to come. It underscores the tension between past grief and future hope, assuring the faithful that God’s blessing can follow even the deepest losses. This enriches the verse’s message of restoration, portraying God as one who turns barrenness into fruitfulness.
